verses.text: Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? Who this who is glorious in his clothing, marching in the greatness of his strength? “It is I who speak in righteousness, mighty to save.”
Why is your clothing red, and your garments like him who treads in the wine vat?

“I have trodden the wine press alone; and of the peoples, no one was with me: Yes, I trod them in my anger, and trampled them in my wrath. Their lifeblood is sprinkled on my garments, and I have stained all my clothing.
For the day of vengeance was in my heart, and the year of my redeemed has come.
I looked, and there was no one to help; and I wondered that there was no one to uphold: therefore my own arm brought salvation to me; and my own wrath upheld me.
I trod down the peoples in my anger, and made them drunk in my wrath, and I poured out their lifeblood on the earth.”

I will tell of the loving kindnesses of Yahweh and the praises of Yahweh, according to all that Yahweh has given to us, and the great goodness toward the house of Israel, which he has given to them according to his mercies, and according to the multitude of his loving kindnesses.
For he said, “Surely, they are my people, children who will not deal falsely;” so he became their Savior.
In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them. In his love and in his pity he redeemed them. He bore them, and carried them all the days of old.
But they rebelled, and grieved his holy Spirit. Therefore he turned and became their enemy, and he himself fought against them.
Then he remembered the days of old, Moses and his people, saying, “Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? Where is he who put his Holy Spirit among them?”
Who caused his glorious arm to be at Moses’ right hand? Who divided the waters before them, to make himself an everlasting name?
Who led them through the depths, like a horse in the wilderness, so that they didn’t stumble?
As the livestock that go down into the valley, Yahweh’s Spirit caused them to rest. So you led your people, to make yourself a glorious name.

Look down from heaven, and see from the habitation of your holiness and of your glory. Where are your zeal and your mighty acts? The yearning of your heart and your compassion is restrained toward me.
For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us. You, Yahweh, are our Father. Our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
O Yahweh, why do you make us wander from your ways, and harden our heart from your fear? Return for your servants’ sake, the tribes of your inheritance.
Your holy people possessed it but a little while. Our adversaries have trodden down your sanctuary.
We have become like those over whom you never ruled, like those who were not called by your name.

footnotes.content: This is the Lord Jesus in his terrible majesty—not the meek lamb we remember, but the warrior who has trampled enemies alone. The prophet sees Him coming from Edom (Esau's land, a symbol of human rebellion), stained red with the wine of judgment. He speaks in righteousness, mighty to save: every act of justice flows from His character.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophet's question cuts straight to the scandal of the Cross: Why such staining? Such cost? The answer lies in Christ's solitary work on our behalf—He stands alone in the wine press of God's wrath so we need not. His garments are dyed not with vanity but with redemption's price.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He trod alone. Not the angels, not the saints—He bore the full weight of judgment by Himself. "My peoples, no one was with Me." Yet this isolation is precisely our salvation: His wrath upheld the work; His anger finished it for us. The staining of His garments becomes the robe of our righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The day of vengeance" and "the year of my redeemed"—two sides of the same coin. Judgment on sin and rescue of sinners happen in one act. This is the gospel's heart: the Lord's wrath against evil becomes the Lord's mercy toward the guilty, all in the sacrifice of the cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I looked, and there was no one to help." In Gethsemane, the cup was His alone to drink. Peter had fallen asleep; God the Father seemed distant; the weight fell entirely on the Son. Yet in that total solitude, His own arm and wrath upheld the eternal plan. Loneliness became love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The judgment is complete. He did not step back or negotiate with evil; He trod it down utterly, poured out all His wrath against sin and death. This finality is our peace—there remains no second judgment for the redeemed, only the steadfast mercy of a Savior who bore it all on our behalf.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From vengeance to mercy—the prophet's heart shifts now to remember. He will tell of Yahweh's loving-kindnesses, not out of obligation but out of wonder at goodness poured out on the house of Israel, and on us too. Gratitude for mercy received becomes the shape of all true worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Surely they are My people, children who will not deal falsely." The Lord's trust in His covenant people is not based on their perfection but on His faithfulness to redeem them. He became their Savior not because they earned it, but because He resolved it. This is the security of adoption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In all their affliction He was afflicted." This echoes the suffering servant who bears our griefs—the angel of His presence (understood in Jewish tradition as the divine messenger, the pre-incarnate Christ) saved them. He bore them, carried them through the wilderness and through all their sorrows. This is God's tenderness made visible in history and in the Cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: And yet they rebelled. Grieved His holy Spirit. This is the tragedy of ingratitude—the people whom He loved and carried turned away, forcing Him to become their adversary and fight against them. Sin is that serious; mercy was that generous; the refusal was that real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prayer turns to memory: "Where is He who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of His flock?" The Exodus is the template. Then Moses led Israel through the Red Sea; the angel of His presence saved them. The question is not really a question—it is trust looking backward, asking the Lord to remember what He has always been.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who caused His glorious arm to be at Moses' right hand?" The Lord's mighty acts in Egypt and at the sea are not accidents or the hero's deeds—they are the Lord Himself acting to make Himself an everlasting name. His miracles are His self-revelation. He moves in history for His glory and our salvation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Like a horse in the wilderness"—steady, sure-footed, never stumbling. The Lord guided them through the deep, chaotic places as if on a familiar road. This is the shepherd's way: He does not shield us from the depths, but He does not let us fall in them either.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "As livestock go down into the valley"—gently, naturally, the Lord's Spirit caused them to rest. This is divine care in the midst of travel: the Lord leads His people not by whip but by the gift of peace. And all of it, all the leading and protecting and resting, was to make Himself a glorious name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Look down from heaven and see." The prayer shifts to present crisis—zeal and mighty acts seem hidden; compassion is restrained. This is the heart's cry when God feels far away. Yet the very fact that the people cry out to Him, asking Him to look and remember, is itself a confession of faith: He is there to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You are our Father." Not Abraham—though he was the covenant father—but the Lord Himself. "Our Redeemer from everlasting is Your name." This is the deepest claim: God's very name, His eternal character, is redemption. We belong to Him not by accident of birth but by His faithful choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why do You make us wander from Your ways?" A hard question, but asked in faith—not accusation but bewilderment. The people sense their own hardened hearts and ask the Lord to reverse it. "Return for Your servants' sake"—they appeal to covenant loyalty, reminding Him that His honor is bound up in the redemption of the tribes of His inheritance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your holy people possessed it but a little while." The sanctuary—that place where God's presence dwelt—has been overrun by adversaries. This is the backdrop of exile, of apparent abandonment. Yet even in loss, the people still call it "Your sanctuary." Despair has not broken their faith that the Lord owns what is broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We have become like those over whom You never ruled, like those who were not called by Your name." Readers today hear an echo in this—we too know the feeling of living as though God's kingdom were distant, as though we were orphans. Yet the very prayer itself—honest, desperate, clinging to the name of God—shows that we have not truly slipped His hold. He is listening still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
